1:
The day that burns as an oven is placed by most of the voices at the fall of Jerusalem rather than at the end of the world. Gill denies that it is the day of judgment, as Kimchi and other interpreters both Jewish and Christian think, and takes it of Christ coming in his kingdom and power to take vengeance on the Jewish nation, which burned both figuratively and literally when their city and temple were burnt about their ears. Clarke agrees and adds the means, whether famine, sword or captivity, and calls neither root nor branch a proverbial expression for total destruction. Wesley hears the refiner's fire of the previous chapter now burning more dreadfully, as it did when the fire raged everywhere but most fiercely where the arched roofs made it double itself and infold flames with flames; and he allows it to stand as an emblem of the day of judgment.

Calvin argues the point. The greater part think the prophet speaks of the last coming of Christ, which does not seem to him probable. He grants that such expressions have not their full accomplishment in this world, but says God so suspends his judgments as never to withhold evidences of them, that the godly may have some props to their faith. He refers the day to the first coming instead: the Jews made a confident boast of the coming of a Redeemer, and are answered that the day would come, but not the day they imagined. He hears irony in the repetition, since the same men had lately called the proud happy while reckoning themselves far from that character. On the last clause he observes that branch is improper where the figure is stubble, branches belonging to trees, the phrase being a proverbial one for everything.

Henry takes the day at both comings, likening it to the pillar of cloud and fire with a dark side turned toward the Egyptians and a bright side toward the Israelites. The proud are fuel because they make themselves stubble, that is, combustible matter; were they gold, silver and precious stones they would abide the fire and be purified by it. Ellicott identifies the day with one already foretold, and notes that the wicked here are not the heathen only but the murmurers themselves, so far from being accounted happy.

On the Sun of righteousness the voices divide. Clarke takes it of the Lord Jesus, and reads the healing in the wings from the sun's rays, which revive and fructify the whole creation, the rays being the truths of his Gospel and the influences of his Spirit. Ellicott grants that the fathers and early commentators who understood Christ are so far right that the period of his advent is meant, but denies any personal reference in the expression, since the word for sun is feminine in Hebrew and the literal rendering is in her wings; he would render the next phrase prance or sport rather than grow up. Wesley keeps the person and observes that the Hebrew word imports mercy and benignity as well as righteousness, a remark Henry makes as well.

Going forth is read historically and generally at once. Clarke recalls that when Cestius Gallus suddenly raised the siege the Christians took the opportunity to escape from Jerusalem to Pella in Coelesyria, so that no Christian life fell in the destruction of the city; but he thinks the words are of more general meaning too, of going forth in all the occupations of life. Henry has souls going forth from their bodies at death and bodies from their graves at the resurrection, and reads the growth as that of calves of the stall, quick and strong and useful, not as the flower of the field which is slender and soon withers. Gill limits the promise to the few of that character among a wicked nation.
3:
Treading down the wicked is read at three different levels. Gill takes it of the saints treading them as grapes in the winepress, as Christ did before them and they by virtue of him, who makes them more than conquerors over all their enemies, spiritual and temporal. Clarke reads it as a military commission and thinks it may be the charge given to the Romans: tread down the wicked people, tread down the wicked place, set it on fire, and let the ashes be trodden down under your feet. Wesley keeps the promise wholly inward, and finds it fulfilled when believers by faith overcome the world, when they suppress their corrupt appetites and passions, and when the God of peace bruises Satan under their feet. Ellicott confines himself to the wording, and would render the clause about the day not as a past act but as one God is about to make.

The charge to remember the law comes with a reason attached, and the voices supply different ones. Gill notes that no other prophet would be sent after Malachi, so that the law was to be their rule and directory in the interval; that Christ, now prophesied of, would be the end of that law; and that the exhortation was the more needed because in the period between this prophet and the coming of Christ the traditions of the elders were invented and obtained, which greatly set aside the law and made it of no effect. Wesley hears the same silence announced and takes it as a leave-taking: they are to have no more prophecy until the great prophet come, and must attend diligently to the law meanwhile. He presses the last words as forbidding a selective obedience, since statutes and judgments mean the whole law and not a part of it, to be remembered as God requires; and he takes the phrase about all Israel to reach as long as they should be a people and a church.

Henry works the charge out at greater length and draws four things from it. Corrupt churches are to be reformed by the written word and reduced to the standard of the law and the testimony; the closing of a book of prophecies does not supersede the law, since the prophets do but confirm and apply it and press the observance of it, so that even when we have made considerable advances in knowledge we must still retain the first principles of practical religion; the coming silence is no real want, for we need not complain for want of visions and revelations as long as we have the written word and the canon of scripture complete to be our guide, that being the most sure word of prophecy and the touchstone by which we are to try the spirits; and those who look for the Messiah are to live in obedience to the light they have, since to him that uses well what he has, more shall be given.

One textual observation stands apart from the exposition. Clarke reports that the Septuagint, the Arabic and the Coptic place this verse last in the book rather than here, and takes the substance of the charge to point back to the things predicted in the law itself. The change of order is not a small one, since it decides whether the prophet closes on a command to remember or on the promise that follows; and Gill, Wesley and Henry all treat the verse where it stands, as an interval charge given because the voice of prophecy is about to fall silent, rather than as the last word of the whole.
5:
The identity of the promised Elijah is settled the same way by every voice, on different grounds. Gill begins with the text, noting that the Septuagint wrongly inserts the Tishbite in place of the word prophet; the person meant is not Elijah himself, who lived in the days of Ahab, but John the Baptist, come in the power and spirit of Elijah. He lists the likeness in temper, in manner of clothing and austere way of living, in courage in reproving vice, and in zeal and usefulness. He rejects the expectation he ascribes to Kimchi and others, that the very Elijah shall come in person before the Messiah the Jews expect, so that difficult questions are left till Elijah comes and solves them; and counts a like expectation among some ancient Christian writers equally groundless. Clarke says the same briefly.

Ellicott argues it out. There is no more reason to suppose Elijah is to appear upon earth than to imagine from the prophecies naming David that he is to come again in the flesh. When the deputies of the Sanhedrim asked John the Baptist whether he was Elias and he answered that he was not, he simply gave a negative reply to a question formulated on their misapprehension. That he is nevertheless the messenger of the earlier promise and the Elijah of this one is shown conclusively, as far as Christians are concerned, by the announcement before his birth, by the accounts of his ministry, and by our Lord assuring the people that John was this messenger and his disciples that he had appeared unrecognised. Ellicott ends by noting that Moses and Elias, named together in this last exhortation, are the two who appeared with Christ on the Mount of Transfiguration.

Wesley measures the interval: though the spirit of prophecy cease for four hundred years, at the expiring of those years one shall be sent as great as Elijah. The great and dreadful day he refers literally to the vengeance upon the Jews, from the death of Christ to the desolation of the city and temple, and only by accommodation to the end of the world. Keil and Delitzsch renders the last clause more narrowly, smiting not the earth but the land, and not with a curse but with the ban.

On the turning of hearts the readings part. Wesley takes it domestically, of the unnatural divisions then among the Jews, in which fathers studied mischief to their own children and children were estranged from them. Ellicott denies any such reference, and will not have it of family disputes such as might arise from marriage with foreign wives; following Keil he takes the fathers for the ancestors of the nation, the patriarchs and the pious forefathers, and the sons for the degenerate descendants of the prophet's own time, and quotes Hengstenberg that the bond of union, the common love of God, is wanting, so that fathers and children are ashamed of each other. Clarke reads the particle as joining rather than dividing, old and young together, and Gill notes that it may be rendered with the children rather than to them.

The close of the book is itself discussed. Clarke glosses the curse as utter extinction, and holds that had the Jews turned to God at the preaching of John and of Christ it would not have been executed. He reports that in most Masoretic Bibles the fifth verse is repeated after the sixth, since the Jews do not like to let their sacred book end with a curse, and that in most manuscripts there are three chapters here, the fourth joined to the third. Ellicott reports the same practice, comparing the endings of Isaiah, Lamentations and Ecclesiastes, to avoid an ending of ill omen. Wesley makes the observation without the remedy, that the last word of the Old Testament is a curse where the New ends with a blessing.
